muc.title: 60 pages of slides
muc.text: Your teacher sends a sixty-page slide file before the exam. You read it from start to finish, then read it again.

muc.title: Rereading loses to answering
muc.text: As part one said, rereading doesn't help you remember as well as answering questions yourself. So turn your materials into exercises.

muc.title: Only uses your materials
muc.text: One tool that does this very well is Google's NotebookLM. You upload slides, PDFs and notes, and it only answers based on exactly those materials.

muc.title: All kinds of exercises
muc.text: One click gives you quizzes, flashcards, mind maps, or an audio summary to listen to on the go.

muc.title: Where you went wrong, where to look
muc.text: Get a quiz question wrong, click explain, and it shows which part of the materials has the right answer.

muc.title: Any app can do it
muc.text: Claude or ChatGPT can do it too: upload the file and ask for questions. The trick is to also ask why each wrong answer is wrong.

muc.title: 10 multiple-choice questions
muc.text: Upload a lecture file and say: make ten multiple-choice questions from this material, ask them one at a time, and if I pick the wrong answer, explain why it's wrong.

muc.title: AI asks you back
muc.text: So far, AI asks and you answer. What about when you ask and AI won't give you the answer? Part four.
